title: Admission-control Reservoir Batch Playbook
body:
Purpose
---
Working scratchpad for a different take on continuous-batching sizing: combine an admission-control "reservoir" concept with tapered concurrency limits to reduce p95 tail while preserving token-unit economics. This doc captures simulation notes, heuristics, spreadsheet links, and a proposed rollout checklist for experiments on staging.

TL;DR recommendations
---
- Default policy for medium-throughput routes (avg QPS 10-200): use a small Reservoir (R = 4 concurrent batches) + windowed batch cap W_ms = 12 ms + per-instance concurrency cap C_max = 8.
- For heavy steady streams (QPS > 300): increase reservoir to R = 8, W_ms = 8 ms, C_max = 16 and enable prefix-KV cache hot-path.
- For spiky low-duty routes (QPS < 5): favor low C_max (2-4) with longer W_ms = 25 ms to capture microbursts into single batch.
- Monitor: p95 latency, queue depth, batch occupancy, and cost-per-token. Aim p95 budget = configured SLO * 0.9 before rollout.

Motivation / intuition
---
Continuous batching reduces per-token GPU compute by amortizing kernel startup and memory copy. But naive continuous batching + high concurrency can produce long queueing tails when arrival processes are bursty. The "reservoir" pattern: maintain a small pool of active batch slots (reservoir size R). New requests can only start a batch if reservoir has free slots. When reservoir is saturated, admission-control applies backpressure (reject or degrade to lower-cost model) rather than letting queueing escalate.
This controls extreme queueing tail while still allowing concurrency to scale across instances. The reservoir is intentionally small (1-10 slots) to keep queuing latency budgets tight.

Simulation notes (event-driven emulation)
---
- Arrival models tested: poisson, two-state Markov (idle/burst), and empirical traces (customer A 2025-03).
- Service-time model: token-generation time approximated by linear function + overhead: service_ms = base_ms + tokens * per_token_ms (base_ms 12ms, per_token_ms 1.2ms for model-16b quantized).
- Batching behavior: batch forms for up to W_ms or max_batch_size. For continuous batching we use W_ms timer and dynamic max based on prefix-match heuristics.
- Concurrency scheduling: when a batch completes, reservoir slot frees. Concurrency per-instance capped by C_max.

Key results summary (spreadsheet rows excerpt)
---
- Markov burst (burst_len 300ms, burst_qps 120): naive continuous (W_ms=10, C_max=32) -> p95 = 760ms, median = 85ms, cost-per-1M-tokens = $52.
- Reservoir (R=6, W_ms=10, C_max=32) -> p95 = 210ms, median = 92ms, cost-per-1M-tokens = $58. Slightly higher cost because some spare capacity wasted, but p95 dramatically improved.
- Tapered C_max (R=6, W_ms=10, C_max=16) -> p95 = 170ms, cost-per-1M-tokens = $61.
- Low QPS (avg 2): long W_ms=25 + R=2 -> reduces number of tiny batches, cost down 18% vs naive while p95 within SLO.

Interpretation and tradeoffs
---
- Reservoir reduces worst-case queueing at the expense of peak utilization; good for customer-facing routes with tight p95 SLOs.
- Tapered concurrency prevents multiplying batch queueing across many in-flight batches. Empirically the sweet spot is C_max ~= 1.5 * R for mixed arrivals, but this varies by model latency curve.
- For cost-sensitive internal workloads where p95 is less critical, prefer larger R and higher C_max to maximize throughput.

Default knobs and suggested defaults (first-pass)
---
- reservoir_size (R): default 4 (range 1-12)
- batch_timer_ms (W_ms): default 12 ms (range 6-50)
- instance_concurrency_cap (C_max): default 8 (range 2-64)
- backpressure_behavior: soft-throttle (preferred) or hard-reject
- degraded_fallback_model: model-small-quant (optional)

Deployment experiment plan (staging -> canary -> prod)
---
1) Implement reservoir admission control as a feature flag (runtime/serving).
2) Run A/B on synthetic trace replay (staging) comparing naive vs reservoir across 3 traffic shapes. Capture p50/p95/p99, cost-per-token, and batch occupancy histograms.
3) Canary: enable for 10% of traffic for a single region, route under conservative defaults. Monitor: p95, error rate, instance utilization.
4) Expand canary to 50% if p95 reduced and error rate stable.
5) Roll to 100% for routes that benefit.

Open questions / TODOs
---
- Admission policy when reservoir saturated: prefer soft-throttle (increase client-side retry hints) vs immediate fallback to smaller model? We need UX and SLA implications. (Action: SRE + Product decision).
- How to auto-tune R per-route based on measured arrival distribution? Proposed metric: reserve R such that P(queueing_delay > budget) < 1% over last 24h. Need an efficient estimator.
- Interaction with autoscaler: if reservoir increases apparent queuing, autoscaler may spin up instances causing feedback loops. Add hysteresis and queue-aware autoscaling signals.
- Spreadsheet to convert simulation outcomes into $/1M-tokens needs to be consolidated with platform billing (linked).

Reference artifacts and spreadsheets
---
- Simulation workbook: gsheets: /sheets/reservoir-sims-2025 (internal) [placeholder].
- Quick cost calc (tab): assumptions: $/gpu-hour = $3.8, avg tokens/sec per instance computed from sim.
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1847 (prototype reservoir admission code).

Action items
---
- [Ava] flesh out estimator for auto-tuning R (due 2025-07-28).
- [Rahul] add queue-aware metric to autoscaler (Spike, due 2025-08-04).
- [Maya] draft product note on fallback UX and SLA implications (due 2025-07-30).

Notes to self
---
- Keep doc intentionally pragmatic; more of a playbook than a theoretical paper. Include more empirical traces (customer B) before finalizing defaults.
- When writing rollout docs for Console, surface reservoir as a per-route toggle with recommended presets (low/mid/high throughput).

End.
